title: Penicillin Pharmacology: Mechanism of Action, Spectrum, Therapeutic Uses and Adverse Effects

notes.text: Penicillin discovered by alexander Fleming in 1928 when he found out that his staphylococcal culture has been contaminated by something that kills the bacteria
Later he found out that was penicillin mold
Penicillin is from cell wall inhibitors class
Pharmacokinetics
Some penicillin types had to be taken IV (benzyl penicillin)
IM penicillin like benzathine penicillin
Some other penicillin that taken oral
If taken oral penicillin then either before or after food by 1 hour
Because most antibiotics get affected by food (should be taken on empty stomach)
When choosing type of penicillin you must take into account type and severity of infection
Penicillin molecular weight 300- 500 according to type of penicillin
Penicillin non ionized in usual form but when it enter the body ph 7.4 turn into ionized compound which can’t cross blood brain barrier except if there is meningitis
blood vessels can leak compounds into peripheral tissues except in brain the cells lining the blood vessels have tight junctions which make them not leaking
But when there is inflammation the vessels in brain start leaking compounds so it leak penicillin
Although penicillin can’t cross blood brain barrier, it can cross the placenta but it is not teratogenic so it is safe in pregnancy because the fetal tissue does not have transpeptidase
Penicillin excreted by kidney except nafcillin and oxacillin which excreted through bile
Probenecid which used to treated gout by increasing the excretion of uric acid lead to decrease excretion of penicillin and leaving it in plasma for longer time
Mechanism of action
Penicillin is group of drugs
Gram positive bacteria cover itself with thick cell wall while in gram negative has thin cell wall
Cell wall consist of peptidoglycan = protein +carbohydrate
Cell wall has multiple glycan units that cross linked to each other by the transpeptidase enzyme by transpeptidation reaction
Mechanism of action 1
Penicillin inhibits the transpeptidase enzyme and lead to dissolving of the cell wall and bacteria become exposed to external environment and lead to lysis by osmotic pressure => bactericidal
Some books call transpeptidase enzyme = penicillin binding protein
Penicillins work on rapidly dividing bacteria
Mechanism of action 2
Penicillin enter the cell and activate autolysin
Autolysin used by the bacterial cell to dissolve its own cell wall during reproduction
So when penicillin activate autolysin leads to more destruction to cell wall and lead to cell rupture and lysis
Penicillin works well with gram positive bacteria because it has developed cell wall
Penicillin works well on actively multiplying bacteria => bactericidal
Penicillin antibacterial spectrum
Various penicillin are active against almost all types of bacteria

Penicillin G is active against gram positives like streptococci, clostridium perfringens (cause gas gangrene), pneumococci and staph that doesn’t produce penicillinase and it is active against gonococci , treponema pallidium
Anti staph penicillin is active against MSSA
Amino penicillins active against penicillin G spectrum and listeria monocytogenes (gram + cause eneterococcal infection) the salmonella (typhoid) and shigella (dysentery) (both gram -)
Anti pseudomonal penicillins active against pseudomonas, and active against multiple gram negatives and some gram positives and anaerobes
Bacteria develops resistance mechanisms to Penicillins, those include natural and acquired resistance
Natural resistance
Natural resistance like in bacteria that lack the peptidoglycan cell wall (mycoplasma pneumonia)
Acquired resistance
Effect of penicillin depends on the beta lactam ring
Some bacteria secrete beta lactamase enzyme (penicillinase) the lead to destruction of the beta lactam ring

We have multiple types of bacteria that secretes beta lactamase including staph aureus , some strains of E coli (penicillinase secreting E coli, pseudomonas, some strains of proteus , some strains of streptococci , H influenza
To avoid that penicillin added to tazobactam, sulbactam or clavulanic acid which are beta lactamase inhibitors
Presence of efflux pump reduce amount of intracellular drug (klebsiella pneumonia)
Therapeutic uses
Penicillin used to treat bacterial infections and it is active against all types of bacteria

The only antibiotic used for prophylaxis benzathine penicillin (long acting) used for prophylaxis against rheumatic fever every 3 to 4 weeks ;; also used for prophylaxis against endocarditis in kids with congenital heart disease caused by strep viridans that infect the heart and cause vegitations on valves ;;; any dental work in patient susceptible to endocarditis should be using pencillin for prophylaxis

Hypersensitivity reactions , 5-10% have hypersensitivity against penicillin ; hypersensitivity range from simple skin rash to angioedema to anaphylactic shock ; patient that might go into anaphylactic shock after taking penicillin is 1/10000 ;;; hypersensitivity reactions might be immediate after 1 to 2 minutes (type I hypersensitivity that might go into anaphylactic shock) after taking the drug or delayed until 12 days (type III hypersensitivity reactions) ;;; sensitivity comes from metabolic products of penicillin after getting metabolized by liver because penicillin works on transpeptidase enzyme which is available in bacteria only;;; sensitivity more with IV route and couldn’t be predicted (ask patient if have penicillin hypersensitivity, or do test were you give the penicillin G intradermally in low dose and watch if there is hypersensitivity reaction in that area then that person have penicillin hypersensitivity) ;;; person might have hypersensitivity originally or developed over time ;;;; you ask about hypersensitivity in history
Seizures, procaine penicillin might cause seizures if given intrathecally
Nafcillin might cause bone marrow depression
Methicillin might cause interstitial nephritis (not used anymore because of MRSA) Co amoxiclav have clavulanic acid which is hepatotoxic
Drug Interactions

Penicillin is bactericidal (destroy cell wall) and better work on the dividing bacteria to kill it by destroying its cell wall, if added with bacteriostatic like erythromycin => erythromycin would make the bacteria static and slow its division making the penicillin not effective
Antipseudomonal penicillin have –ve charged and when mixed with positive charge like aminoglycosides both deactivated like piperacillin and gentamicin

title: Penicillin Classification Explained: Penicillin G, Anti Staph, Amino & Antipseudomonal Penicillin

notes.text: We have four types of penicillin
First is benzyl penicillin (penicillin G)
Second is antistaph penicillin (beta lactam resistant penicillin)
Extended spectrum penicillin (aminopenicillins)
Antipseudomonal penicillin
Benzyl penicillin (penicillin G)
Is the original penicillin that discovered by Fleming
First used in 1942
It effective against gram positives like streptococci (upper respiratory tract infections), pneumococci (pneumonia), staphylococci that doesn’t produce penicillinase
It is active against gonococci (cause gonorrhea) which is gram negative; treponema pallidum (cause syphilis), clostridium perfringens (cause gas gangrene)
Not given orally , only IV form
Half life from 2-4 hours (short half life) so if someone have pneumonia they would take 10 injections per day
Dissolve by beta lactamse enzyme
The only penicillin that is calculated by units because it is natural material because every natural material calculated by units but if we change in it then calculated by mg
Modifications to Penicillin G
If adding procaine to penicillin it extends it half life to 12-24 hours and it is called procaine penicillin

Benzathine if added penicillin stay in body 3-4 weeks and it is called benzathine benzyl penicillin or benzathine penicillin G (long acting penicillin) and this is given to kids with recurrent tonsillitis and might have rheumatic fever so give them long acting penicillin and it is taken IM only 1.2-2.4 million units; it is used in prophylaxis and used in treating syphilis in pregnancy
It also get modified to be taken orally and it is called penicillin V (could be given orally) (phenoxy methyl penicillin)
Anti-staph penicillin (beta lactamase resistant penicillin)

Modification so it become resistant to lactamase; penicillinase resistant penicillin (antistaph penicillin) and include methicillin, cloxacillin, dicloxacillin, floxacillin, nafcillin (bile) and those would be active against staph only (narrower spectrum than original form); and it is not used alone because of the spectrum, it is used with other antibiotics to broaden the spectrum like amoxicillin and floxacillin; and even the staph sometimes not affected by it (MRSA)
Not used anymore because it cause interstitial nephritis
Amino penicillins (extended spectrum penicillins)

Extension of the spectrum: original penicillin works well with gram + and you want it to work with gram -; gram negative have outer membrane that highly selective; the idea was to make the penicillin look like amino acid to trick the gram negative bacteria and the result was extended spectrum penicillin (amino penicillin) examples are ampicillin and amoxicillin

Ampicillin and amoxicillin are broad spectrum active against positive and negative bacteria and could be given orally; they are active against penicillin g spectrum and shigella, salmonella (3 advantages); disadvantage include the fact that they are vulnerable to beta lactamase enzyme (staph, Neisseria, pseudomonas, E coli, proteus, H influenza)

To improve that, they took the ampicillin and amoxicillin and mixed it with clavulanic acid or sulbactam or tazobactam (which are beta lactamase inhibitors) and examples for those include co amoxiclav (co combination amoxicillin and clavulanic acid) also has another name which is amoxicillin, Unasyn (sulbactam + ampicillin)

Amoxicillin vs ampicillin: both could be given orally but amoxicillin better absorption orally, distribution of amoxicillin is better reaching the respiratory system better, chance of diarrhea as side effect is higher with amp than amox because the absorption is lower so it reaches the intestine more; both have the same spectrum but ampicillin is more active against shigella which cause dysentery, amoxicillin is more active against salmonella (cause typhoid)
To solve problems of ampicillin. Pro drugs of ampicillin like (talampicillin, Pivampicillin) dissolve in intestine in inactive form and when enter the circulation liver metabolize it into active form
Anti pseudomonal penicillin
Examples: ticarcillin, azlocillin, mezlocillin, piperacillin (best one)
Active against pseudomonas, also active against multiple gram negatives and some gram positives and some anaerobes
Available in IV formulations only
Expensive drugs for highly resistant pseudomonas
Used for wound sepsis in diabetic patients, diabetic foot
It becomes even more effective when added to aminoglycosides (NH2) work on gram negative so the mix kills all gram negative bacteria

Antipseudomonal penicillins are negatively charged while aminoglycosides are positively charged so when mixed in same syringe they deactivate each other and preferred to be given in separate syringes in separate sites
This group of penicillins also affected by beta lactamase enzyme, also added to clavulanic acid or tazobactam or salbactam and tazobactam + piperacillin available as tazocyn

title: How to Choose Antibiotics (Antibiotic Prescription): Patient Factor and Drug Factor

notes.text: Antibiotics are prescribed according to the Five Rights, Five rights include:

The right patient: confirm presence of infection; fever, CBC, special test;;; fever is hallmark of every bacterial infection of 37.2 C except if patient is immunocompromised and fever does not always mean patient have infection ;;; CBC you look for WBC (5000- 10000), neutrophil 60%- 70% of WBC and it fight bacteria , lymphocytes 30% fight viruses and TB, eosinophil 4-10% allergic or parasitic infection , basophil <1% it elevates in leukemia and lymphoma ;;; specific test => you
You approach is that you determine if there Is a fever or no and what caused the fever like infectious cause, cancer .. You want to confirm you do CBC and specific test
Right drug: when we choosing the right drug we need to consider type infective organism, patient factors, tissue penetration
Identification of infective organism

1- ideally you want to know the infective organism (you take infective material and you send it to lab) like CSF fluid specimen if you sus meningitis and you send for culture and sensitivity ; urine if you sus UTI => lab would tell you the infective organism and what drugs it is susceptible for

But sometimes you give antibiotic without knowing the infective organism and that is what we call empirical therapy and we only give empirical therapy in acutely ill patient because the culture and sens takes 2-3 days and you can’t wait that long with these patients;;; also you give empirical therapy in patients who have neutropenia (<5000) because these patients are immunocompromised;;; and you give empirical therapy in patients who have meningitis (usually have severe headache, photosensitivity, neck rigidity) you give penicillin for these patients and then you take CSF for culture and sensitivity

When selecting empirical therapy drug you want to take into consideration site of infection and patient’s history (previous infections, age, recent travel hx, recent antimicrobial therapy, immune status, whether infection is hospital or community acquired)

2- patient factors: some antibiotics can’t be used in some age groups; neonates can’t be give chloramphenicol or sulfonamide, chloramphenicol cause grey baby syndrome, sulfonamides cause kernicterus;; children can’t be given tetracyclines cause abnormal teeth formation (dental enamel hypoplasia), fluoroquinolones cause articular damage;;; old age can’t be given aminoglycosides because it cause severe nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity ;;; pregnant patient can’t take aminoglycosides cause congenital deafness, fluroquinolones it pass placenta and cause articular damage; immunocompromised patient can’t take bacteriostatic drugs because they arrest growth and wait for immune system to clear bacteria but this patient is already immunocompromised so no point of giving that;;; people with renal dysfunction need dose adjustment and careful monitoring of the concentration so the drug does not accumulate same for hepatic dysfunction

3- tissue penetration: antibiotic must reach site of infection so the infection get irradicated. in case of chronic abscess – antibiotic can’t go through the lining of the abscess because it is fibrous tissue so no point of giving antibiotics ;;; diabetic foot there is ischemia so antibiotic can’t reach the ischemic parts unless excision and debridement of the ischemic part ;;; natural barriers like blood brain barrier, blood eye barrier, blood prostate barrier; in case of blood brain barrier you give the drug intrathecally or being able to cross that barrier (high lipid solubility, low molecular weight)

In summary regarding right drug we explained that we need to know that type of organism through culture and sensitivity of the infected material and you make sure that the drug you want to use is good for your patient age group and health condition and you make sure that the drug you want to choose is going to reach the tissue infected

Minimal inhibitory concentration: minimum concentration of antibiotic required to inhibit the microorganism; below MIC antibiotic unable to kill bacteria;;; and according to the MIC antibiotics categorized into

Concentration dependent killing: antibiotic kills the microorganism more when concentration increased like gentamicin from aminoglycosides so it is given in high oral doses compared to others (80, 160mg)
Time dependent killing: killing of microorganism more if antibiotic stayed in circulation more like penicillin so it is given more frequently like 4 times a day every 6 hours

Post antibiotic effect: some antibiotic still have the killing effect even if its concentration in plasma diminished because it is aggregated in the infection sites and inside microphages like fluoroquinolones that aggregates in infection sites and macrolides (azithromycin)
Patients with severe infection better given antibiotics parenterally
Mild infections better with oral
Every infection have treatment duration that is already allocated by general guidelines
Acute rhinosinusitis is 5 days duration of treatment; acute otitis media 5- 7 days, community acquired pneumonia 5- 7 days
After complete resolution it is better to continue the antibiotic for another 2- 3 days to prevent relapse
And if relapse happen then the infection is back and bacteria is resistant towards the antibiotic you already used
